pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Matter Cycling in Ecosystems

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-LS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS2-1].

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 'Interactions and interdependencies' / 'Material cycles'):** the role of decomposers and the recycling of materials/nutrients through an ecosystem underpins the KS3 carbon cycle this topic feeds into.

- **Operational details:** The pivotal idea: MATTER CYCLES (it is recycled, never used up) whereas ENERGY FLOWS one way and is lost — the pairing that most sharpens both. Pupils build a model tracing atoms/nutrients: soil nutrients → taken up by a plant → eaten by an animal → animal dies (or produces waste) → DECOMPOSERS (fungi, bacteria, worms) break it down → nutrients returned to soil → available to plants again. The decomposer is the load-bearing, most-forgotten node: without it the loop doesn't close and nutrients would lock up in dead matter. Pupils must describe the decomposer's role, trace matter around the full loop, and interpret/create a cycle diagram. This is the KS2 model that KS3's carbon and water cycles specialise.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (relational/systems). Pupils model a closed loop and articulate that matter is recycled while energy is not. Success = traces matter through the full cycle including decomposers and explains why the cycle would break without them.
bestPractices: Teach matter cycling and energy flow together and in contrast — matter loops, energy is one-way — because the contrast defines each.
Give decomposers centre stage as the loop-closing step, confronting the common omission head-on with a 'what if nothing rotted?' scenario.
Trace a concrete parcel of matter (a nutrient atom) all the way around so 'cycle' means a literal return, not a vague flow.
Use a closed-loop diagram (not a linear chain) so pupils see the end feeds the beginning.
Connect forward to KS3: this general matter loop is what the carbon and water cycles specialise.
keyRepresentations: Closed-loop cycle diagram: soil → plant → animal → dead matter → decomposer → soil
A followable nutrient parcel travelling around the loop
Decomposer close-up (fungi/bacteria/worms on a rotting log) returning nutrients
Side-by-side one-way energy stream vs closed matter loop
commonMisconceptions: Thinking matter is 'used up' and gone, rather than recycled endlessly through the ecosystem.
Omitting decomposers, so the cycle appears not to close and dead matter just vanishes.
Conflating matter cycling with energy flow — believing energy also cycles back, or that matter is lost like energy.
Assuming plants get their mass/matter mainly from the soil rather than understanding nutrient uptake as one part of a wider cycle.

learn.summary: For learners aged 10–11, build a model of matter cycling in ecosystems that traces a single parcel of nutrients around a closed loop (soil → plant → animal → dead matter → decomposers → soil) and contrasts the recycling of matter with the one-way flow of energy with heat transferred out of the ecosystem. The pivotal ideas: matter is recycled and never used up, while energy flows one way and is transferred out as dispersed heat, not destroyed; and decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) are the loop-closing node without which the cycle cannot complete. Learners describe the decomposer's role, trace matter through the full loop, and interpret or create a cycle diagram. This KS2/5-LS2-1 model is the foundation that KS3's carbon and water cycles later specialise.

activities.title: Drive a nutrient parcel around the matter cycle
feedback: If a learner says the dead material 'disappears' or 'rots to nothing', point out that decomposition rearranges matter rather than destroying it — the material moves into the soil, the air, and the decomposers' own bodies, and is all still there.

If a learner describes decomposers only as things that 'eat dead stuff', agree that they do feed on dead matter (so in that sense they are consumers too), then add what sets them apart: as they feed, decomposers break dead remains and wastes down into simple substances released into the soil (and air) that plants can take up again — that release is what closes the loop.

If a learner says plants eat soil or make matter from nothing, explain that roots take in water and mineral nutrients, while the carbon used to make sugars and much of the plant’s dry biomass comes from carbon dioxide in the air through photosynthesis. Matter is taken in and rearranged, not created from nothing.
If a learner thinks energy also cycles back, revisit the energy stream: it enters from the sun and leaks away as heat and never returns, unlike the matter loop.
activities.rationale: Following one parcel is intended to make 'cycle' mean a real return rather than a vague flow, and switching decomposers off confronts the most common omission directly — learners can see the consequence of a broken loop. A closed-loop structure (not a linear chain) shows that the end feeds the beginning, and the parallel energy stream makes the matter-cycles-vs-energy-flows contrast concrete.
sourceClaims: Decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil, closing the matter cycle; matter is recycled through an ecosystem while energy flows one way and is lost.
learnerActions: Follow a single labelled 'parcel' of nutrients as it moves out of the soil, into a growing plant's roots, into an animal that eats the plant, into the animal's dead remains, then into the decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) that break it down and hand the nutrients back to the soil — where the same parcel is taken up by the next plant.
At each step, state what matter is moving and which process moves it.

Turn the decomposers OFF and describe what happens: dead leaves and bodies pile up, nutrients stay locked in dead matter, the soil's available nutrients deplete, and new growth stalls because the loop no longer closes.
Explain in your own words why decomposers are the step that CLOSES the loop and why matter is recycled rather than consumed.
Watch a parallel one-way energy stream — sunlight entering and heat leaking away, never returning — and state the contrast: matter cycles, energy flows.
activities.intendedInsight: A cycle is a literal closed loop: the same matter returns to the beginning and is used again. Decomposers are the load-bearing step that closes the loop; without them nutrients lock up in dead matter. Matter is recycled endlessly, whereas energy flows one way and is transferred out of the ecosystem as dispersed heat, not destroyed.

activities.title: Read and build a closed-loop cycle diagram
feedback: If the learner draws a linear chain that stops at dead matter or at the decomposer, prompt: where do those returned nutrients go, and what takes them up next?
If the decomposer node is missing, ask what breaks down the dead matter and returns its nutrients — without it the arrow back to soil has no cause.
Check that labels name both the process and the matter moving, not just the organisms.
activities.rationale: Interpreting and creating a cycle diagram is part of the stated evidence and the NGSS modelling standard. A tappable or lift-the-flap canonical diagram is a strong pre-teach and reference, but as a fixed representation it cannot be manipulated to break the decomposer step and observe the loop fail, so it is best paired with the active model where that consequence can be tested.
learnerActions: Study a labelled cycle diagram of soil → plant → animal → dead matter → decomposer → soil, and for each node and arrow state the process happening and what matter is moving.
Pay particular attention to the decomposer node — describe how fungi, bacteria and worms on a rotting log return nutrients to the soil.
Then construct your own cycle diagram from scratch, ensuring the end arrow feeds back into the beginning so the loop is genuinely closed.
Mark where new plant growth draws on the returned nutrients.
activities.intendedInsight: A canonical closed-loop diagram is the shared representation for matter cycling; being able to both read and produce one, with decomposers included, shows the loop actually closes.

activities.title: 'What if nothing ever rotted?' discussion and thought experiment
feedback: If a learner only describes things 'piling up', push toward the consequence for new growth: with nutrients locked in dead matter, the available soil nutrients deplete and plants can't get what they need.

Reward answers that recognise decomposers feed on dead matter and break it down into simple nutrients released back to the soil for plants (unlike animals that mainly eat living things), and that correctly say the same nutrient can cycle round repeatedly.
activities.rationale: A guided thought experiment or soil-ecologist-style dialogue is a useful extension that may make the decomposer insight explicit through reasoning and talk; it complements, rather than replaces, the dynamic loop model where the closed-loop behaviour can be observed directly.
sourceClaims: Decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil, closing the matter cycle; matter is recycled through an ecosystem while energy flows one way and is lost.
learnerActions: Discuss or write a response to: 'What would happen to a forest if there were NO decomposers?'
Talk through how a decomposer differs from an ordinary animal that just eats.
Reason aloud about whether the same nutrient can be used more than once in an ecosystem, and explain how.
Trace one nutrient from a dead tree into a living plant to show matter is not destroyed when things rot.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning about a no-decomposer ecosystem reveals the decomposer's loop-closing role by exposing what breaks without it, and reinforces that matter is conserved and recycled.

activities.title: Check and discriminate the model
feedback: Full understanding: matter is conserved and cycles — decomposers return nutrients to soil, taken up by plants, passed to animals, back to decomposers — and the learner can reason about a no-decomposer ecosystem.

Partial: knows decomposers break down dead matter and can trace part of the chain, but treats it as disposal rather than recycling, or cannot close the loop back into new plants — revisit the return-to-soil step.
Gap: thinks rotting matter is destroyed or sees decomposers as mere eaters — re-establish conservation of matter and the recycling role before moving on.

The 'is it destroyed?' question separates learners who think rotting matter vanishes from those who conserve it; the decomposer question separates 'just eats rubbish' from 'recycles nutrients back into the soil'.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, selection and discrimination tasks check the model efficiently; the layered prompt separates the conservation misconception from the decomposer-role misconception. Because these verify rather than build the model, they should follow the constructive activities and be paired with explanatory tasks.
learnerActions: Sequence the stages of the matter loop in order.
Answer targeted questions such as 'What returns nutrients to the soil?' and sort processes by what they do.
Decide which quantity is recycled and which is lost (matter cycles vs energy flows), and justify the choice.

Respond to this prompt: 'A fallen tree rots away on the forest floor until you can barely see it. Where has all its material gone — is it destroyed? Explain what the decomposers did with it, and how that material can end up in a new plant.'
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can trace the full loop including decomposers, conserves matter, and keeps matter cycling distinct from energy flow. These checks verify the model; they do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing the loop or explaining the decomposer role in their own words.

activities.title: Decomposition up close (optional tangible extension)
feedback: Keep the focus on the systems loop: after observing, have the learner place what they saw back onto the cycle diagram so the tangible detail reconnects to the recycling logic.
activities.rationale: A soil-profile dig or close-up of a rotting log can make decomposition vivid and concrete, and the carbon/water cycles that KS3 covers are specialisations of this same matter loop. A hands-on close-up offers a different experience from a screen model; the two are complementary, since the target here is the systems loop and the close-up supports — rather than substitutes for — tracing matter around it.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 covers the role of decomposers and the recycling of materials through ecosystems, extending the KS2 matter-movement model into the carbon cycle.
learnerActions: Examine decomposers at work — for example fungi, bacteria and worms on a rotting log, or a short look 'under the soil' at a decomposing layer.
Connect what you observe to the cycle: name what the decomposers are breaking down and what they return to the soil.
Relate this general matter loop forward to the carbon and water cycles you will meet later, which are specific versions of the same idea.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing real decomposition can make the abstract node tangible and links the systems loop to concrete organisms and to later carbon/water cycle study.

constraints: Target age 10–11; conceptual systems-thinking (relational/Tier B) objective: trace matter through the full cycle including decomposers and explain why the cycle would break without them.
Teach matter cycling and energy flow together and in contrast — the contrast defines each.
Use a genuinely closed-loop representation, not a linear chain, so the end feeds the beginning.
Include decomposers explicitly as the loop-closing step; a model or diagram that omits them does not meet the objective.

A fixed cycle diagram (tappable or lift-the-flap) is a strong canonical reference and pre-teach, but being static it cannot be manipulated to break the decomposer step and observe the loop fail; pair it with an activity where the consequence of a broken loop can be reasoned about or observed.

Recognition and sequencing tasks check the model but do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing the loop or explaining the decomposer's role in their own words; include constructive and explanatory tasks too.

A tangible soil dig or rotting-log close-up and a screen-based loop model offer different experiences; treat the tangible work as an extension that reconnects to the systems loop, not as a replacement for tracing matter around it.

Avoid implying plants get most of their mass from soil. Roots take in water and mineral nutrients; the carbon used to build sugars and much of the plant’s dry biomass comes from carbon dioxide in the air through photosynthesis.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any activity was tested.

The source claim that decomposers return 'some carbon to the air' (in the source's correct-answer text) is biologically sound for a fuller picture but goes slightly beyond the KS2 soil-nutrient focus; it is retained in context but not emphasised in learner-facing steps for this age.

One source claim (decomposer role / energy-flows statement) is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited to support the teaching principle but its specific wording should be treated as background, not independently confirmed, pending review.

The DfE KS3 claim supports the forward-connection to carbon/water cycles and is cited only on the extension activity that makes that link, not on the diagram-building task it only matched on topic grounds.

The legacy entry asserted the dynamic 2D model is where 'the concept lands' and that static diagrams 'can't' teach the loop-breaking insight; this has been softened to a scoped affordance (static diagrams cannot be manipulated to show the loop failing) rather than a claim that only one medium teaches the concept.

Internal assessment vocabulary ('two-tier', 'diagnostic') was removed from learner-facing wording in the check activity and replaced with plain language; the underlying prompt and discrimination logic are unchanged.
Worms are grouped with fungi and bacteria as 'decomposers' following the source; strictly they are detritivores, but the grouping is conventional and acceptable at KS2.

probeDeeper: If matter isn't destroyed when things rot, follow one nutrient from the dead tree into a living plant.
What would happen to a forest if there were NO decomposers?
How is a decomposer different from an ordinary animal that just eats?
Can the same nutrient be used more than once in an ecosystem? How?
assess.correctAnswer: The material is NOT destroyed. Decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) break the dead tree down, returning its nutrients to the soil (and some carbon to the air). Those soil nutrients are taken up by new plants' roots and passed on to animals that eat the plants — so the matter cycles round again. Nothing is lost; it is recycled through the ecosystem.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The rotting material just disappears / rots away to nothing' — matter not conserved.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that decomposition rearranges matter, it doesn't destroy it: the material moves into soil, air and decomposer bodies, all still there.
errorPatterns.distractor: The rotting tree's material just disappears — it rots away to nothing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the dead tree's material is gone or destroyed once it rots.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Decomposers just eat dead things / are gross rubbish-eaters' — misses the recycling-to-soil role.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast with an ordinary consumer: decomposers break dead matter down AND return its nutrients to the soil for producers — that recycling is the point.
errorPatterns.distractor: Decomposers just eat the dead wood — they don't put anything back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes decomposers only as eating, never as returning nutrients to the soil.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'New plants make their material from nothing' or 'plants eat soil as food' — cannot correctly source the new plant's matter.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Route the recycled nutrients into the plant via roots (with photosynthesis for carbon); matter is taken up, not created.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot say where the new plant's material comes from, or says the plant 'eats' soil like food.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks rotting matter is destroyed; sees decomposers as mere eaters.
responseLevels.full: Models matter as conserved and cycling — decomposers return nutrients to soil, taken up by plants, passed to animals, back to decomposers — and reasons about a no-decomposer ecosystem.
responseLevels.partial: Knows decomposers break down dead matter and can trace part of the chain, but treats it as disposal rather than recycling, or cannot close the loop back into new plants.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A fallen tree rots away on the forest floor until you can barely see it. Where has all its material gone — is it destroyed? Explain what the decomposers did with it, and how that material can end up in a new plant.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'Is it destroyed' separates a child who thinks rotting matter simply vanishes from one who conserves it. The decomposer tier separates a child who thinks decomposers 'just eat rubbish' from one who knows they RECYCLE nutrients back into the soil for new growth.
